name: install knex with mysql2
desc: Knex has no driver of its own. mysql2 is the package that opens MySQL sockets, so both go into dependencies.
body: The `client` value does two jobs: it picks the SQL dialect and it names the driver module. `mysql2` is the maintained driver. `mysql` is the old one and differs on big integers and decimals.

name: knex()
desc: Creates a query builder factory with its own connection pool. Call it once per process, in a module you import everywhere.
body: A `knex()` call per request is the classic bug. Each call builds another pool, MySQL counts the connections, and the error is `ER_CON_COUNT_ERROR: Too many connections`.

name: knexfile
desc: Configuration file the knex CLI and the app share. Keyed by environment, so credentials stay out of code.
body: Older examples put `dateStrings` at the top level. It belongs in `connection`, because mysql2 reads it. Pick the block with `config[process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development']`, and give the CLI the same file: `npx knex migrate:latest --knexfile knexfile.cjs --env production`.

name: pool
syntax: pool: { min, max, acquireTimeoutMillis, idleTimeoutMillis, afterCreate }
desc: Bounds how many MySQL connections this process holds. Without a cap, load creates sockets until the server refuses them.
body: `waitForConnections` is true by default, so queries queue when every socket is busy. One slow query holding all ten turns into a pile of waiters that time out together. Lower the pool or fix the query. Raising `max` only moves the failure into MySQL.

name: db.destroy()
desc: Closes every pooled socket. A script that forgets this prints its result and then hangs, because an open socket keeps the event loop alive.

name: select()
desc: Lists the columns to return. The result is an array of plain objects with one key per column.
body: Two tables with a `name` column produce one key that overwrites the other in the object. Alias at least one side.

name: where()
desc: Adds an AND condition. Values travel as bindings, so quotes in the value cannot change the statement.
body: `where('phone', null)` builds `phone = NULL`, which is never true and returns no rows. Use `whereNull`. An empty array in `whereIn` produces a false condition, so the query returns nothing instead of failing.

name: orderBy() with limit()
desc: Sorts and pages the result. Offset and limit map to the MySQL `LIMIT m, n` clause.
body: A column name from the query string must be checked against a whitelist before it reaches `orderBy`. Identifiers are not bindings, and quoting is not validation.

name: first()
desc: Runs the query with `LIMIT 1` and resolves to one row, or to `undefined` when nothing matches. No array to unwrap.

name: count()
desc: Returns an aggregate row. MySQL sends COUNT as BIGINT, which mysql2 can hand over as a string, so convert before doing arithmetic.
body: `count()` on a builder that already has `limit` counts at most that many rows. Build the count query from a fresh `db(table)`.

name: insert()
desc: Writes one row or many. On MySQL it resolves to `[insertId]`, an array whose first item is the auto increment value.
body: The bookings table has a composite primary key and no auto increment, so an insert id comes back as 0. Do not treat it as the key of the new row.

name: update()
desc: Updates the rows the builder selects and resolves to the number of affected rows.
body: MySQL counts changed rows, not matched rows. Sending the same values again returns 0, so 0 means either no row or no difference. A `select` in the same transaction tells them apart. An empty patch object makes knex throw.

name: del()
desc: Deletes the selected rows and resolves to how many were removed. `truncate()` is the fast, unrollbackable alternative.
body: `del()` with no `where` deletes every row and reports no error. Guard the route, and keep `truncate()` for seeds and tests.

name: returning()
desc: Asks for the written row back. MySQL has no RETURNING clause, so knex warns and ignores it. Read the insert id or select again instead.

name: onConflict()
desc: Turns an insert into MySQL's upsert: `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` for merge, `INSERT IGNORE` for ignore.
body: MySQL ignores the column list you pass, because `ON DUPLICATE KEY` fires on any unique key of the table. Know which keys exist before you rely on it. `merge()` with no column list updates every inserted column.

name: join()
desc: Adds an inner join. Only rows with a match on both sides survive.
body: Always alias and qualify. Two joined tables with a `name` column give an ambiguous column error, and unqualified `select('*')` silently drops one of them from the result object.

name: leftJoin()
desc: Keeps every row from the left table, with `null` on the right side when nothing matches. Use it for lists that include zero counts.
body: Putting a right-side condition into `where` removes the `null` rows, so the query behaves like an inner join. Use the join callback, or accept `whereNull` as the alternative.

name: groupBy()
desc: Collapses rows into groups so aggregates can be computed per group. MySQL 8 rejects plain selected columns that are missing from the group list.
body: `SUM` and `AVG` on MySQL come back as DECIMAL, which mysql2 returns as a string. Wrap them in `Number()` before arithmetic or before sending them in JSON.

name: db.transaction()
desc: Runs statements on one connection as a unit. Resolving commits, throwing rolls back.
body: Using `db(...)` inside the callback runs on a different socket, outside the transaction, so a rollback leaves that write in place. Every statement inside must use `trx`. A deadlock (`ER_LOCK_DEADLOCK`) is safe to retry once, from outside the callback.

name: raw()
desc: Sends SQL you write yourself, still with bound values. On MySQL it resolves to `[rows, fields]`, not to rows.

name: whereRaw()
desc: Adds a raw condition. `?` binds a value and `??` binds an identifier, and the difference decides whether the query works.
body: The `%` and `_` characters inside user input stay wildcards even when bound. Escape them, or accept that a search term can match more than it should.

name: schema.createTable()
desc: Builds tables from code in a migration. Types, keys, and constraints are methods on the table builder.
body: Drop in reverse creation order in `down()`, because MySQL refuses to drop a table another table still references. The composite key form is `table.primary(['customer_email', 'hotel_id'])`.

name: migrate:latest
desc: Runs every migration that is not in the `knex_migrations` table yet. Rollback undoes the last batch.
body: The bookkeeping table is `knex_migrations` by default. Give each app its own `tableName` when two apps share a database, or one app will skip the other's files.

name: seed:run
desc: Fills a development database with test rows. Seeds run in filename order, which is why they are numbered.

name: err.code
desc: mysql2 puts a stable MySQL error code on the error object. Branch on the code, because the message text changes between versions and languages.
body: Knex adds `error.sql` and `error.bindings` to driver errors. Log them on the server only. `sqlMessage` is a schema map for anyone who can read the response.
